client: I've been feeling really off ever since my breakup with Maria about three months ago. Things I used to love, like going hiking with my friends on the weekends, just don't feel enjoyable anymore — I kind of dread it now, or I just make excuses not to go. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a try.
therapist:
Thank you for giving this a try — it takes courage to show up even when part of you isn't sure it will help. It sounds like the breakup has left a quiet but heavy weight on your life, slowly dimming the things that used to bring you joy, like those weekend hikes. That kind of gradual withdrawal can feel confusing, almost like you're watching yourself from a distance.

Can you tell me a little more about what goes through your mind in those moments when a hike comes up and you start looking for a reason not to go?

client: Honestly, it's kind of hard to pin down exactly what happens in those moments. It's like my brain just starts listing all these reasons why today isn't the right day — I'm too tired, the weather looks off, I haven't been sleeping well — but underneath all that I think there's this feeling that going alone would just make it worse, like it would remind me of all the times we used to go together. And then I feel guilty for even avoiding it, like I'm letting myself down on top of everything else.
therapist:
What you're describing makes a lot of sense — your mind is working overtime to protect you from pain, generating all those practical-sounding excuses so you don't have to face the deeper ache of missing what you and Maria shared on those trails. But then that layer of guilt sneaks in on top, so you end up feeling stuck between two uncomfortable places. That pattern — avoiding to escape pain, then feeling bad about avoiding — is something we can really work with together.

When you imagine actually going on one of those hikes, what's the specific moment or image that feels the hardest to sit with?

client: Honestly, the hardest image is probably reaching the top of the trail — that specific overlook where Maria and I used to sit and just talk for hours. I can almost picture turning to say something to her and then realizing she's not there, and that emptiness feels unbearable. I don't know if I'm ready to feel that in real life, not just in my head.
therapist:
That image is so vivid and specific — it speaks to how much meaning that place holds for you, and it makes complete sense that your mind wants to protect you from that moment of reaching out and finding her gone. What's worth noticing, though, is that you're already feeling that emptiness right now, just by imagining it, which tells me you're carrying this with you whether you go on the hike or not. 

I'm wondering — when you sit with that image of the overlook, what does that emptiness seem to say to you about yourself, or about what your life looks like going forward?

client: I guess... when I picture standing there alone, it's like the emptiness is telling me that this is just what my life is now. Like she was the person I did everything with, and without her, all those places just become reminders of what I've lost instead of things I actually enjoy. It's hard to imagine the overlook ever feeling like anything other than a monument to her being gone.
therapist:
There's something really significant in what you just said — that the overlook has become a "monument," as if that place, and maybe others too, have been permanently redefined by loss rather than belonging to you. That's a painful and heavy story to be carrying, and it's worth gently examining whether that story is a fact or a conclusion your grieving mind has drawn. 

What evidence do you have that those places *can't* ever hold new meaning for you — and is there any part of you, even small, that isn't fully convinced by that story?

client: I mean... I hear what you're saying, and maybe you're right that it's a conclusion rather than a fact. But when I try to imagine going back there with someone else, or even alone, it just feels like a betrayal somehow, like I'd be erasing what we had. And I guess that's the part I can't get past — the idea that making new memories there would mean the old ones matter less.
therapist:
There's something really tender in what you're protecting here — the fear that moving forward somehow diminishes what you and Maria had, as if the value of those memories depends on keeping everything frozen around them. But I'd gently invite you to consider whether the opposite might also be true: that those memories already exist, complete and real, and nothing you do at that overlook can actually reach back and change what they meant. 

What do you think it would say about you *as a person* if you were able to eventually return there and still carry those memories with you, rather than having to avoid the place to prove they mattered?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that... but it also feels like you're making it sound easier than it is. Like, if I go back there and I'm okay, does that mean I've just... moved on? That I don't miss her as much anymore? I guess I'm scared that being okay with it would feel like a betrayal, even if logically I know that doesn't quite make sense.
therapist:
You're not being illogical at all — there's something deeply human about equating pain with love, as if the ache of missing her is proof that she mattered. But I want to offer a gentle reframe: being okay doesn't mean you've stopped loving or missing her, it means you've found a way to carry that love without it costing you everything you once enjoyed. Healing and loyalty can actually coexist.

What would it mean to you if missing her and eventually feeling okay could both be true at the same time?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's true. But it almost feels like... if I let myself be okay, I'm admitting that life just goes on without her, and that feels really cold to me. Like the world shouldn't just keep spinning like nothing happened.
therapist:
There's something really profound in what you're feeling — like being okay would mean the world is indifferent to something that mattered enormously, and that feels almost unbearable to accept. But I wonder if there's a difference between the world *not noticing* and *you* carrying forward the weight of what she meant to you — because you moving through life doesn't make you indifferent, it actually takes a kind of quiet courage.

What do you think Maria would make of the idea of you slowly finding your way back to the things you love?

client: I've thought about that before, actually — what Maria would want for me. And honestly, part of me knows she'd hate seeing me like this, she was always pushing me to get out more, to stop isolating myself. But then there's this other part that feels like... if I start enjoying things again, it's like I'm proving that life just goes on without her, and that feels like a betrayal somehow.
therapist:
It's really meaningful that you already know, somewhere inside you, what she would want — and that part of you hasn't been able to give yourself permission to honor that yet. It sounds like you're caught between two kinds of love: one that holds on by staying still, and one that honors her by living the way she believed you could. 

What would it feel like to think of enjoying life again not as proof that it goes on *without* her, but as carrying a piece of her forward with you?

client: That's... a really different way to think about it, and part of me wants to hold onto it. But honestly, it also feels a little too neat, like a nice idea that might not survive contact with an actual good day where I laugh at something and then immediately feel sick about it. I guess I'm scared that even if I tell myself I'm "carrying her forward," in the moment it won't feel like that at all — it'll just feel like I forgot her for a second.
therapist:
That fear is so honest and real — and you're right that a reframe can sound clean in a conversation but feel completely different when you're in the middle of a genuine laugh and then that wave of guilt crashes in. What you're describing, that "I forgot her for a second" feeling, is actually one of the most common and painful parts of grief, and it doesn't mean the framework is wrong, it means grief is messy and nonlinear. That moment of forgetting isn't a betrayal — it's just proof that you're still alive.

When that sick feeling has hit you before after a good moment, what has that inner voice actually said to you — and do you think it's been telling you the truth?

client: The inner voice usually says something like "how dare you laugh when she's gone" or "you don't actually miss her as much as you thought you did." And honestly, in those moments, it feels completely true — like I've just caught myself in some kind of lie about how much I loved her. I know logically that's probably not right, but logic doesn't really show up when the guilt hits.
therapist:
That voice is incredibly harsh — essentially putting you on trial for the crime of being human for a moment, and it's no wonder logic can't compete with that when the guilt hits so fast and so hard. In CBT we'd call that an automatic thought, and what's worth noticing is that it's not a neutral observer reporting facts — it's a prosecutor that only presents one side of the evidence. The fact that you can laugh doesn't disprove your love; if anything, your capacity for joy is part of what made those years with her meaningful.

When you imagine talking to a close friend who was grieving and laughed for a moment, would you let that same voice speak to them — and if not, what would you say to them instead?
